title: Distortions in Judged Spatial Relations
research_question: To what extent do subjects' judgments of relative geographical relations exhibit systematic distortions, particularly when locations are in different geographical or political units, and can these distortions be explained by a hierarchical representation of spatial information?

participants.description: Undergraduate students from the University of California, San Diego (10 in Exp 1, 10 in Exp 2A, 12 in Exp 2B, 14 in Exp 3).
participants.recruitment: Volunteered in response to campus advertisements (Exp 1, 2A, 2B) or participated as part of a course requirement (Exp 3).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Questionnaire with textual descriptions of 5 real-world geographical location pairs (e.g., Portland, Ore. to Toronto) and 15 filler pairs. Subjects drew directions on a circle.

Simple maps (21.6 × 21.6 cm) showing 3 cities (x, y, z) within 1 or 2 'counties'. Conditions: Homogenous (no county lines between key cities), Congruent (city direction matches county direction), Incongruent (city direction opposite county direction). Tested for horizontal and vertical dimensions.
Simple maps similar to Exp 2A, but with 4 cities, adjusted county lines (vertical for incongruent), and a non-interfering county line for homogenous condition. Included 8 filler maps.

Simple maps with 2 key cities (x, y) and 2 filler cities within 2 counties. Manipulated superordinate direction (East-West vs North-South) and deviation of city direction from superordinate direction (15, 45, 75 degrees). Maps were projected on a screen (1m x 1m).

measures.instrument: Drawing a line on a circle to indicate direction (measured in degrees)
Binary choice (e.g., 'Is x east or west of y?')

mechanisms: Spatial information is stored hierarchically, with relations between regions explicitly stored only if they are part of the same superordinate unit.
Relations between regions not explicitly stored are inferred by combining relations between superordinate units and relations of subregions within their respective superordinates.
The inference process may weight higher-level (superordinate) information more heavily than lower-level information.

Distortions arise because the level of processing necessary for precise encoding or inference is typically not performed, leading to reliance on coarser, superordinate representations (e.g., 'northwest quadrant').
moderators: Amount of stimulus deviation from superordinate direction (15, 45, 75 degrees)
implementation_implications: Higher-order organizational structure in spatial information cannot be ignored as it causes systematic errors in judgments about spatial relationships.
Organizational units for spatial information are not limited to political regions and depend on the ultimate use of the stored information (e.g., airline pilots might use routes and political units).

limitations: None explicitly stated by authors as a dedicated section; however, the authors address and refute potential limitations such as perceptual illusions and guessing strategies.

environmental_features: Names of geographical locations (cities, states, countries)
control_conditions: Comparison of judgments for geographically 'congruent' location pairs (where within-unit and between-unit directions align) versus 'incongruent' pairs (where they conflict).

theory_commitments.specific_claim: People organize spatial information hierarchically, and judgments about the relative positions of subordinate units (e.g., cities) are biased by the relative positions of their superordinate units (e.g., states), especially when these relations conflict.

mechanism_chain.description: The proposed cognitive mechanism suggests that when individuals judge the spatial relation between two subordinate geographical locations, they first access the superordinate units (e.g., states) containing these locations. The retrieved spatial relation between these superordinate units then biases or distorts the judgment of the subordinate locations, particularly when the direct subordinate relation conflicts with the superordinate one.

steps.from_construct: Request for spatial relation between subordinate locations

steps.to_construct: Retrieval of spatial relation between superordinate units
Bias/distortion in judged spatial relation between subordinate locations

instruments_used.name: Direction Judgment Task
instruments_used.construct: Judged spatial relations; cognitive map distortions
instruments_used.description: Participants were presented with pairs of geographical locations and asked to judge their relative direction (e.g., 'Is X north or south of Y?').

stimulus_images.description: Diagrams illustrating geographical locations (e.g., San Diego, Reno, California, Nevada) and their superordinate units, used to explain the hierarchical organization and potential distortions.
